claim: PARP1 is an important player in the response to DNA damage.
source: Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) is an important player in the response to DNA damage.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: HPF1 was shown to be a critical modulator of the activity of PARP1 by facilitating PARylation of histones.
source: Recently, Histone PARylation Factor (HPF1) was shown to be a critical modulator of the activity of PARP1 by facilitating PARylation of histones and redirecting the target amino acid specificity from acidic to serine residues.
evidence: This statement references recent findings that are cited in the introduction.

claim: HPF1 redirects the target amino acid specificity from acidic to serine residues.
source: Recently, Histone PARylation Factor (HPF1) was shown to be a critical modulator of the activity of PARP1 by facilitating PARylation of histones and redirecting the target amino acid specificity from acidic to serine residues.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and confirmed by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: HPF1 provides the catalytic base Glu284 to substantially redirect PARylation by PARP1.
source: HPF1 provides that catalytic base Glu284 to substantially redirect PARylation by PARP1 such that the histones in nucleosomes become the primary recipients of PAR chains.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments and activity assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Histones in nucleosomes become the primary recipients of PAR chains in the presence of HPF1.
source: HPF1 provides that catalytic base Glu284 to substantially redirect PARylation by PARP1 such that the histones in nucleosomes become the primary recipients of PAR chains.
evidence: This is demonstrated by gel-based PARylation assays shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: HPF1 partitions most of the reaction product to free ADP-ribose (ADPR).
source: Surprisingly, HPF1 partitions most of the reaction product to free ADP-ribose (ADPR), resulting in much shorter PAR chains compared to reactions in the absence of HPF1.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC assays shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: HPF1 results in much shorter PAR chains compared to reactions in the absence of HPF1.
source: Surprisingly, HPF1 partitions most of the reaction product to free ADP-ribose (ADPR), resulting in much shorter PAR chains compared to reactions in the absence of HPF1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by AMP-PR quantitation in Figure 6D.

claim: PARP1 and PARP2 serve as early detectors of DNA damage.
source: The abundant nuclear proteins poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 and 2 (PARP1 and PARP2) serve as early detectors of DNA damage (Gibson and Kraus, 2012; Ray Chaudhuri and Nussenzweig, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: PARP1, upon binding to damaged DNA, binds NAD+ and transfers the ADP-ribose (ADPR) portion onto itself and other proteins.
source: PARP1, upon binding to damaged DNA, binds NAD+ and transfers the ADP-ribose (ADPR) portion onto itself and other proteins.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of PARP1 action.

claim: Histones are the most abundantly PARylated proteins apart from PARP1.
source: These PAR chains are attached to thousands of nuclear proteins with histones being the most abundantly PARylated proteins apart from PARP1 (Bonfiglio et al., 2017a; Larsen et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Histone-linked PARylation depends on Histone PARylation Factor 1 (HPF1).
source: More recently it has been shown that histone-linked PARylation depends on Histone PARylation Factor 1 (HPF1) (Gibbs-Seymour et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: HPF1 not only promotes transPARylation of histones but also alters the specificity of the modified residues from aspartate or glutamate to serine.
source: Interestingly, HPF1 not only promotes transPARylation of histones but also alters the specificity of the modified residues from aspartate or glutamate to serine (Palazzo et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference and confirmed by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of PARP1 leads to increased carcinogenesis.
source: Deletion of PARP1 leads to increased carcinogenesis, and deletion of both PARP1 and its most closely related homolog, PARP2, is embryonically lethal (Amé et al., 1999; Ménissier de Murcia et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Deletion of both PARP1 and PARP2 is embryonically lethal.
source: Deletion of PARP1 leads to increased carcinogenesis, and deletion of both PARP1 and its most closely related homolog, PARP2, is embryonically lethal (Amé et al., 1999; Ménissier de Murcia et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Four clinically approved PARP inhibitors (olaparib, rucaparib, niraparib, and talazoparib) are in use for treatment of breast and ovarian cancer.
source: PARP1 (and PARP2) are important targets for cancer therapy with now four clinically approved compounds (olaparib, rucaparib, niraparib, and talazoparib) in use for treatment of breast and ovarian cancer (Yi et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: All clinically relevant inhibitors of PARP bind in the NAD+ binding pocket of the catalytic domain of PARP1 and PARP2.
source: All clinically relevant inhibitors of PARP bind in the NAD+ binding pocket of the catalytic domain of PARP1 and PARP2 (Thorsell et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: PARP1 catalyzes four different reactions.
source: From a mechanistic point of view, PARP1 is a very complicated enzyme that catalyzes four different reactions (Alemasova and Lavrik, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Glu988 on PARP1 mediates the deprotonation and activation of the 2′-OH on the acceptor ADPR for PAR chain extension.
source: In the second reaction catalyzed by PARP1, NAD+ is used to extend the initially attached ADPR, wherein the 2′-OH (the acceptor hydroxyl) of this ADPR is deprotonated by Glu988 (Ruf et al., 1998; Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: PARP1 builds long PAR chains of up to 200 units on itself.
source: Repeating this process, PARP1 builds long PAR chains of up to 200 units on itself with a large range reported for average chain lengths (Kawaichi et al., 1981; Sugimura and Miwa, 1982; Alvarez-Gonzalez and Jacobson, 1987), in competition with PARGs (Pascal and Ellenberger, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Branching occurs about once every 5–20 residues for autoPARylation.
source: Branching has been shown to occur about once every 5–20 residues for autoPARylation (Alvarez-Gonzalez and Jacobson, 1987; Miwa et al., 1979) and is mechanistically feasible because of the pseudo-symmetry of ADPR that allows for binding of the elongating polymer in the opposite direction (Ruf et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: PARP1 hydrolyzes NAD+ to generate free ADPR in a 'treadmilling' reaction that becomes more dominant at extended reaction times and low concentrations of NAD+.
source: In the fourth and final reaction, PARP1 hydrolyzes NAD+ to generate free ADPR. This 'treadmilling' reaction becomes more dominant at extended reaction times and low concentrations of NAD+ (Bauer et al., 1986; Desmarais et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Nucleosomes bind tightly to PARP1 (1–13 nM).
source: We have previously shown that nucleosomes bind tightly to PARP1 (1–13 nM) (Clark et al., 2012; Muthurajan et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: HPF1 binds fivefold more tightly to a PARP1–nucleosome complex than to PARP1 bound to a DNA oligomer.
source: Of special relevance to both nucleosomes and HPF1, we have recently shown that HPF1 binds fivefold more tightly to a PARP1–nucleosome complex than to PARP1 bound to a DNA oligomer (Rudolph et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: All nucleosome complexes and free DNA bind to PARP1 with low nanomolar affinity.
source: We found that all nucleosome complexes as well as free DNA bind to PARP1 with low nanomolar affinity as measured in a competition experiment using fluorescence polarization (FP; Table 1, CC50 values).
evidence: This is supported by the competition binding experiments presented in Table 1.

claim: The Km for NAD+ is not affected by the activator.
source: By varying the concentration of NAD+, we determined that the Km for NAD+ is not affected by the activator (Figure 2C) and our Km values are in reasonable agreement with previous determinations of Km of NAD+ for PARP1 (30–100 µM) using a variety of different assay methods (Ruf et al., 1998; Desmarais et al., 1991; Miranda et al., 1995; Langelier et al., 2008; Jiang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Nuc165 consistently yielded a higher turnover number (kcat) than p18mer (p<0.0001).
source: We noted that Nuc165 consistently yielded a higher turnover number (kcat) than p18mer (p<0.0001), and these values are in reasonable agreement with previous determinations (Ruf et al., 1998; Desmarais et al., 1991; Miranda et al., 1995; Langelier et al., 2008; Jiang et al., 2010) of kcat for PARP1 (0.3–5 s−1; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D and Table 1.

claim: All nucleosome complexes tested have similar, higher values of kcat compared to free DNA.
source: Note that p165mer and p621mer DNA fragments, used to assemble Nuc165 and LE-Tri nucleosomes, respectively, have kcat values that are similar to p18mer, whereas all the nucleosome complexes tested have similar, higher values of kcat (Table 1) despite having different lengths of overhanging DNA (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Table 1.

claim: There is a unique aspect of the PARP1–nucleosome interaction compared to the PARP1-free DNA interaction that leads to more robust autoPARylation.
source: We conclude that there is a unique aspect of the PARP1–nucleosome interaction compared to the PARP1-free DNA interaction that leads to more robust autoPARylation, and that this feature is independent of the type of nucleosome.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comparative kcat values shown in Table 1.

claim: In the presence of HPF1 and Nuc165, there is no significant change in the Km for NAD+ or the kcat for incorporation of ADPR into protein compared to the absence of HPF1.
source: Using Nuc165 and adding HPF1 in the plate-based assay described above, we saw no significant change in the Km for NAD+ or the kcat for incorporation of ADPR into protein compared to the absence of HPF1, although the linearity of the assay was significantly reduced compared to assays in the absence of HPF1 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; note the non-zero intercepts with linear fits from 0 to 100 s).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: HPF1 reduces autoPARylation and mediates transPARylation of histones and HPF1.
source: These gels confirm that HPF1 reduces autoPARylation and mediates transPARylation of histones and HPF1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel-based assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No PARylation of histones (or H3 peptide) is detected in the absence of HPF1.
source: It is important to note that we do not detect any PARylation of histones (or H3 peptide) in the absence of HPF1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel-based assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: AutoPARylation is consistently decreased by factors of 2–4 by the addition of HPF1, regardless of which nucleosome is used as an activator.
source: AutoPARylation is consistently decreased by factors of 2–4 by the addition of HPF1, regardless of which nucleosome is used as an activator (Figure 3B, C, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B, C and Table 1.

claim: The presence of HPF1 makes histones in the nucleosome substrates the dominant recipient of PARylation.
source: The presence of HPF1 clearly makes histones in the nucleosome substrates the dominant recipient of PARylation (Figure 3B, C, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B, C and Table 1.

claim: The switch in specificity from autoPARylation towards transPARylation is minimally two- to fourfold.
source: Despite the limitations of this assays, we conclude that the switch in specificity from autoPARylation towards transPARylation is minimally two- to fourfold (Table 1).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data shown in Table 1.

claim: Neither the HPF1-dependent decrease in autoPARylation nor the large switch in specificity is observed using p18mer DNA and H3 tail peptide as a substrate.
source: Neither the HPF1-dependent decrease in autoPARylation nor the large switch in specificity is observed using p18mer DNA and H3 tail peptide as a substrate, presumably because of the weaker interaction of HPF1 with the PARP1–p18mer complex vs. the PARP1–Nuc165 complex (Rudolph et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C and Table 1, and the cited reference.

claim: A very small amount (<0.1 equivalents) of incorporation of ADPR onto HPF1 is observed in the presence of nucleosomes but not free DNA.
source: Additionally, we see a very small amount (<0.1 equivalents) of incorporation of ADPR onto HPF1 in the presence of nucleosomes but not free DNA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Treatment with hydroxylamine removes >90% of ADPR from PARP1 in the absence of HPF1.
source: Treatment with HA removes >90% of ADPR from PARP1 in the absence of HPF1, as seen in a representative gel and by quantitation from replicate experiments (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the presence of HPF1, PARylation on both PARP1 and H3 tail peptide is retained (>90%) after exposure to hydroxylamine.
source: In the presence of HPF1, PARylation on both PARP1 and H3 tail peptide is retained (>90%) after exposure to HA (Figure 3D), indicating the linkages to ADPR are no longer via Asp/Glu and most likely to Ser, as previously reported (Bonfiglio et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3D and the cited reference.

claim: Glu284 is the catalytic base required for PARylation of serine residues.
source: The loss of transPARylation and the retention of binding to the PARP1–Nuc165 complex indicated that Glu284 is the catalytic base required for PARylation of serine residues (Figure 4A), whereas Asp283 is required for a productive interaction of HPF1 with the PARP1–Nuc165 complex.
evidence: This is supported by the mutagenesis and binding data shown in Figure 4 and Table 2.

claim: Asp283 is required for a productive interaction of HPF1 with the PARP1–Nuc165 complex.
source: The loss of transPARylation and the retention of binding to the PARP1–Nuc165 complex indicated that Glu284 is the catalytic base required for PARylation of serine residues (Figure 4A), whereas Asp283 is required for a productive interaction of HPF1 with the PARP1–Nuc165 complex.
evidence: This is supported by the mutagenesis and binding data shown in Figure 4 and Table 2.

claim: The E284A mutant of HPF1 bound significantly tighter (p<0.0001) to the PARP1–Nuc165 complex than wild-type HPF1 (135 vs. 790 nM).
source: Interestingly, the E284A mutant bound significantly tighter (p<0.0001) to the PARP1–Nuc165 complex than wild-type HPF1 (135 vs. 790 nM; Figure 4D, Table 2), validating its structural integrity and ability to recognize the PARP1–Nuc165 complex despite not promoting transPARylation activity.
evidence: This is supported by the binding data shown in Figure 4D and Table 2.

claim: The D283A mutant of HPF1 showed no detectable formation of a complex with PARP1–Nuc165 (KD >10,000 nM).
source: However, only three of these mutants retained their binding to the PARP1–Nuc165 complex (Figure 4C, D), with the D283A mutant of HPF1 showing no detectable formation of a complex (KD >10,000 nM).
evidence: This is supported by the binding data shown in Figure 4C, D and Table 2.

claim: Nuc165 (in the absence of HPF1) yields approximately twofold higher turnover of NAD+ and formation of nicotinamide than p18mer (12.5 vs. 5.4 µM in 1 min).
source: First, in agreement with both the plate-based and gel-based radioactive assays described above, Nuc165 (in the absence of HPF1) yields approximately twofold higher turnover of NAD+ and formation of nicotinamide than p18mer (12.5 vs. 5.4 µM in 1 min; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the HPLC data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Addition of HPF1 increases the overall turnover of NAD+ to form free nicotinamide by a factor of four in the presence of Nuc165 (47 vs. 12.5 µM in 1 min).
source: Addition of HPF1 increases the overall turnover of NAD+ to form free nicotinamide by a factor of four in the presence of Nuc165 (47 vs. 12.5 µM in 1 min; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the HPLC data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the absence of HPF1, 10–14% 'treadmilling' is observed.
source: In the absence of HPF1, we observe 10–14% 'treadmilling', while in the presence of HPF1, PARP1 spends most of its catalytic power (~90%) consuming NAD+ to form free ADPR.
evidence: This is supported by the HPLC data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the presence of HPF1, PARP1 spends most of its catalytic power (~90%) consuming NAD+ to form free ADPR.
source: In the absence of HPF1, we observe 10–14% 'treadmilling', while in the presence of HPF1, PARP1 spends most of its catalytic power (~90%) consuming NAD+ to form free ADPR.
evidence: This is supported by the HPLC data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The E284A mutant of HPF1 has the same effect on the hydrolase activity of PARP1 as wild-type HPF1, even though it neither promotes transPARylation nor serine PARylation.
source: Surprisingly, the E284A mutant of HPF1, which binds more tightly than wild-type HPF1, has the same effect on the hydrolase activity of PARP1, even though it neither promotes transPARylation nor serine PARylation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the HPLC data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Neither wild-type HPF1 nor the E284A mutant have detectable levels of NAD+ hydrolase activity on their own.
source: Control experiments demonstrated that neither wild-type HPF1 nor the E284A mutant have detectable levels of NAD+ hydrolase activity on their own.
evidence: This is based on control experiments performed as part of the study.

claim: Providing high concentrations of the H3 tail peptide substrate suppressed the treadmilling effect to baseline levels in the presence of HPF1 while subtly increasing the overall activity of PARP1.
source: Providing high concentrations of the substrate peptide suppressed the treadmilling effect to baseline levels in the presence of HPF1 while subtly increasing the overall activity of PARP1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: PAR chains are much shorter in the presence of HPF1 than in its absence.
source: If we compare the incorporation of AMP-PR ('middles') at the end of the reaction when all of the NAD+ (200 µM initially) has been consumed, we confirm that the PAR chains are much shorter in the presence of HPF1 than in its absence.
evidence: This is supported by the AMP-PR quantitation shown in Figure 6D.

claim: HPF1-mediated PARylation is not limited to addition of a single ADPR (MARylation) as significant concentrations of AMP-PR are observed that can arise only through true polymerization (minimally trimers).
source: To be noted, HPF1-mediated PARylation is not limited to addition of a single ADPR (MARylation) as we do observe significant concentrations of AMP-PR that can arise only through true polymerization (minimally trimers; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: HPF1 or the E284A mutant alone did not exhibit significant phosphodiesterase activity.
source: Control experiments demonstrated that HPF1 or the E284A mutant alone did not exhibit significant phosphodiesterase activity.
evidence: This is based on control experiments performed as part of the study.

claim: Nucleosomes are better activators of PARP1 than free DNA because there may be direct interactions between the unfolded HD domain and nucleosomes that stabilize the open conformation.
source: Based on the seminal work by Pascal and Black demonstrating that DNA activation of PARP1 is mediated by a series of conformational changes that disorder the HD domain and thereby open up the active site for binding of NAD+ (Dawicki-McKenna et al., 2015; Steffen et al., 2016), we hypothesize that nucleosomes are in some way more efficient in this process. Perhaps there are direct interactions between the unfolded (or alternatively folded) HD domain and nucleosomes that stabilize the open conformation and prevent this domain from collapsing back onto the catalytic domain.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the observed data and cited references.

claim: The PARP1–HPF1 complex has two catalytic bases: Glu284 on HPF1 mediates the deprotonation and activation of serine residues, while Glu988 on PARP1 mediates the deprotonation and activation of the 2′- or 2′′-OH on the acceptor ADPR.
source: The PARP1–HPF1 complex has two catalytic bases. Glu284 on HPF1 mediates the deprotonation and activation of serine residues on acceptor proteins for the initiation reaction (Figure 4A), while Glu988 on PARP1 mediates the deprotonation and activation of the 2′- or 2′′-OH on the acceptor ADPR for PAR chain extension or branching, respectively (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is based on the experimental data and mechanistic understanding presented in the manuscript.

claim: The occurrence of a shared active site formed by PARP1 and HPF1 is a completely unexpected and novel finding in the field of post-translational modification.
source: The occurrence of a shared active site formed by PARP1 and HPF1 is a completely unexpected and novel finding in the field of post-translational modification (Suskiewicz et al., 2020a).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: HPF1 blocks PAR chain formation by occluding the extension site on PARP1.
source: Given that increasing PARylation acceptor sites (i.e., high concentrations of H3 histone tail peptide, Figure 5D) greatly reduces the percentage of free ADPR formed, we conclude that HPF1 blocks PAR chain formation by occluding the extension site on PARP1 (Suskiewicz et al., 2020b), and thus PARP1, still bound to activating DNA (i.e., nucleosome), quickly runs out of suitable PARylation sites and therefore uses water as a nucleophile instead.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data shown in Figure 5D and the cited reference.

claim: PARP1, still bound to activating DNA, quickly runs out of suitable PARylation sites and therefore uses water as a nucleophile instead.
source: Given that increasing PARylation acceptor sites (i.e., high concentrations of H3 histone tail peptide, Figure 5D) greatly reduces the percentage of free ADPR formed, we conclude that HPF1 blocks PAR chain formation by occluding the extension site on PARP1 (Suskiewicz et al., 2020b), and thus PARP1, still bound to activating DNA (i.e., nucleosome), quickly runs out of suitable PARylation sites and therefore uses water as a nucleophile instead.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data shown in Figure 5D and inference from the mechanism.

claim: The high consumption of NAD+ by PARP1 suggests that PARP1 not only plays a role in the DNA damage response but also in metabolic homeostasis.
source: The high consumption of NAD+ by PARP1 suggests that PARP1 not only plays a role in the DNA damage response but also in metabolic homeostasis (Hurtado-Bagès et al., 2020; Murata et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references and the observed data.

claim: PARP1 is the major consumer of NAD+ in the nucleus.
source: PARP1 is the major consumer of NAD+ in the nucleus, and the rapid depletion of the NAD+ pool (50–80%) by PARP1 in response to DNA damage leads to ATP depletion, has dramatic consequences for mitochondria, and leads to cell death via apoptosis and necrosis (Berger, 1985).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The rapid depletion of the NAD+ pool (50–80%) by PARP1 in response to DNA damage leads to ATP depletion, has dramatic consequences for mitochondria, and leads to cell death via apoptosis and necrosis.
source: PARP1 is the major consumer of NAD+ in the nucleus, and the rapid depletion of the NAD+ pool (50–80%) by PARP1 in response to DNA damage leads to ATP depletion, has dramatic consequences for mitochondria, and leads to cell death via apoptosis and necrosis (Berger, 1985).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The observation of partitioning away from PARylation and towards ADPR formation by HPF1 suggests a more important role for ADPR than anticipated as a signaling molecule in its own right.
source: The observation of partitioning away from PARylation and towards ADPR formation by HPF1 is a novel finding that suggests a more important role for ADPR than anticipated as a signaling molecule in its own right (Perraud et al., 2001; Qi et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references and the observed data.

claim: HPF1-mediated PARylation yields much shorter chains than the typical long chains seen during autoPARylation in the absence of HPF1.
source: The conversion of PARP1 into an NAD+ hydrolase is also evident in the much lower incorporation of chain 'middles' onto histones or PARP1 (Figure 6D), indicating that HPF1-mediated PARylation yields much shorter chains than the typical long chains seen during autoPARylation in the absence of HPF1.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: HPF1-mediated PARylation in cells leads primarily to mono-ADPR on serine residues, in part due to the activity of the glycohydrolase PARG.
source: Additionally, it is interesting to compare our findings with a recent demonstration that HPF1-mediated PARylation in cells leads primarily to mono-ADPR on serine residues, in part due to the activity of the glycohydrolase PARG (Bonfiglio et al., 2020), which interestingly also generates ADPR.
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: PARG has been shown to mediate transPARylation of histones, in part by competing with PARP1 for PAR chains.
source: PARG has also been shown to mediate transPARylation of histones, in part by competing with PARP1 for PAR chains (Ménard et al., 1990; Thomassin et al., 1992; Lagueux et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: The formation of shorter PAR chains using either wild-type HPF1 or its E284A mutation is readily understandable given that HPF1 partially occupies the binding site typically associated with PAR chain extension.
source: As concluded for the high hydrolase activity, these shorter PAR chains using either wild-type HPF1 or its E284A mutation are readily understandable given that HPF1 partially occupies the binding site typically associated with PAR chain extension (Suskiewicz et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference and the observed data.

claim: HPF1-mediated PARylation has few if any branch points.
source: Although our assay did not allow us to measure chain branches with sufficient sensitivity, we would argue that for this same reason HPF1-mediated PARylation has few if any branch points.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism by which HPF1 blocks the extension site.

claim: PARP1 is one of the very first proteins recruited to DNA damage sites induced by laser microirradiation, whereas HPF1 arrives more slowly.
source: Also, PARP1 is one of the very first proteins recruited to DNA damage sites induced by laser microirradiation, whereas HPF1 arrives more slowly (Aleksandrov et al., 2018; Mahadevan et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: It is possible that substantial PARylation at some points in time, at some sites, or at some types of damage occurs without HPF1.
source: Thus, it is possible that substantial PARylation at some points in time, at some sites, or at some types of damage occurs without HPF1.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the differential recruitment kinetics of PARP1 and HPF1.

claim: PARP1-alone-mediated autoPARylation leads to long and branched chains, whereas HPF1-mediated PARylation leads to short, most likely unbranched chains.
source: PARP1-alone-mediated autoPARylation leads to long and branched chains, whereas HPF1-mediated PARylation leads to short, most likely unbranched chains.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data and mechanistic understanding presented in the manuscript.

claim: The change in the PARylation pattern may result in the recruitment of different repair proteins to DNA damage sites with HPF1 vs. those without, and thus in turn may direct DNA damage to be repaired by one pathway over another.
source: This change in the PARylation pattern may result in the recruitment of different repair proteins to DNA damage sites with HPF1 vs. those without, and thus in turn may direct DNA damage to be repaired by one pathway over another.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional consequences of the observed differences in PARylation patterns.
